findings.claim: Feature-enabled execEvalStmt creates shared queryBudget and restores final total series/sample counts from it in a defer, including abort paths. Child runSubquery/step-invariant evaluators receive the same budget pointer.

Selected float consumption charges1; selected histogram consumption charges HPoint.size(). That method computes (histogram.Size()+8)/16, relative to float-point units rather than one unit per histogram object.
consumeSamples accumulates with saturating addition and enforces positive maxSamplesRead with strict >. consumeMatrixSamples refuses nil budget or negative step.

For matrix materialized from subquery, caller passes readStep=-1, and outer result does not increment the selected underlying-read charge again. Child source consumption already entered shared budget.

Budget-enabled evalSubquery sets consumer.Range=0 before per-step read merge; helper consumingStep then attributes child steps without requiring them to lie within an outer range window. This preserves selected child work in gaps, with fixed-at special case attributed once.
Step-invariant child is evaluated once; selected samplesRead merge increments at outer step0, while total-sample statistics may repeat at each outer step. These counters are not interchangeable.

documentation_disposition: Preserve engine-input-unit wording and selected child-work/reuse distinction. Avoid physical storage I/O, bytes transferred, each raw decoded point exactly once globally, result count or all-query-branches claims.
remaining_limits: No actual query, iterator, histogram values or storage reads measured; no upstream tests executed.
Histogram.Size internals not expanded; only selected HPoint relative-size formula established.
Full evaluator branch correctness, overflow behavior across all stat merges and all nested special-function cases not exhaustively verified.
Code comments saying storage I/O do not override the actual selected evaluator counter semantics.
This completes a bounded D6 subtopic, not full acceptance of all three large documentation pages.
